title: Small steps beat perfect plans
summary: Why iterative shipping beats waiting for the ideal design — with a few ways to play with the ideas below.

blocks.text: Most essays about productivity start with a confession. Here is mine: I have abandoned more perfect outlines than I have published articles. The gap between intention and shipping is not laziness — it is fear dressed as standards.
This page is both a short essay and a demo: each section is a tile, and each tile can carry its own interactive layer. Use the buttons above or arrow keys to move around.
One voice wants a flawless narrative arc. The other wants to learn something from real readers. They rarely agree on timing.
The first draft is just you telling yourself the story.

pairs.hidden: It means changing the artifact in public view — notes, prototypes, posts — instead of only changing the plan in private.

pairs.prompt: What is the risk of waiting?
pairs.hidden: You optimize for a fantasy audience. Feedback arrives when the cost of change is higher.

blocks.text: Below is the same idea in three modes: compact steps, a checklist, and a slower narrative. Pick what matches your energy today.

sections.title: Step 1 — Capture
sections.body: Write the messy thesis in one screen. No links, no research rabbit holes.

sections.title: Step 2 — Separate
sections.body: Move supporting facts into a second section so the spine stays readable.

sections.title: Step 3 — Share
sections.body: Publish to a trusted circle before you polish the prose for strangers.

blocks.text: Tabs are useful when two perspectives are both true — for example, emotional versus analytical framing.

tabs.label: Emotional
tabs.content: Iteration soothes anxiety because motion beats rumination. Each small release proves you are allowed to exist in the conversation.

tabs.label: Analytical
tabs.content: Iteration reduces variance. Early feedback tightens the loop between hypothesis and evidence, which is the core of any learning system.

tabs.label: Practical
tabs.content: Ship a draft, note one confusion, fix that confusion, repeat. Complexity is deferred until the structure earns it.

blocks.text: Some steps look interchangeable until you try them in the wrong order. Drag items or use the arrows, then check.

interaction.prompt: Put these in a sensible order for a first blog post:
items: Draft the spine in plain language
Cut the clever sentence that repeats the headline
correctOrder: Draft the spine in plain language

blocks.text: If this were your post, you would end with one concrete action. Here is a tiny carousel of endings — swipe mentally with the arrows.

slides.title: Soft ending
slides.body: Try one imperfect paragraph tomorrow morning. Delete nothing for the first fifteen minutes.

slides.title: Direct ending
slides.body: Pick a single reader. Write the last paragraph as an email to them.

slides.title: Playful ending
slides.body: Reward yourself with a nicer heading font only after the second draft is live.
